newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gold Fields on edge after wretched Q3.
newsitem.headline: Gold Fields on edge after wretched Q3.

text.p: Grim third quarter results have divided analysts as to the future of Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd, the world's second largest gold producing company.
Some analysts said the mining house, pushed to the brink by dire September quarter earnings, was staring into an abyss without management offering a strategy to draw it back.
Others said that industry hazards beyond the group's control had razed profits and that Gold Fields had started to implement plans which could bring about better December quarter results.
Gold Fields on Monday posted earnings before capital spending of 274.41 million rand for the third quarter -- sharply down from 355.86 million rand in the second quarter.

The company -- whose output was ranked second in the world by the Gold Fields Mineral Services 1996 report -- attributed its profit fall to fires, which shut off higher grade areas, and a spate of violent industrial action, which halted production.
Gold Fields' three gold mines produced 21,172 kg of gold in the September quarter, down from the 23,021 kg in the preceding quarter.
"They certainly had a poor quarter, but this was a result of factors out of the control of management directly," Dave Giese, analyst at Smith Borkum told Reuters.
"They certainly were in the forefront of all the disasters that one could anticipate in the gold mining industry: labour problems, seismic events and fires in high grade areas.

"They are getting back into areas where the fires occurred, they have made alternative arrangements to access these areas and I do believe that we will see a better December quarter as a result of a higher gold production coming through," he said.
But other analysts accused Gold Fields of sitting back and blaming its troubles on an "unfair world".

"All the others (mining houses) give you an indication of what their strategy is. Gold Fields doesn't seem to have a plan. We can't keep moaning about it not being a perfect world. Everybody knows that and other companies manage to perform.

"Strikes are a symptom of where the company is at. They are not expected to turn around in the short-term," said an analyst who asked not to be identified, adding that the group's earnings were lower than even his bottom-end forecast.
Another analyst said that the market had litle confidence in Gold Fields' management, which played everything "very close to their chest", offering no output or profit forecasts.

Giese agreed: "Management don't appear to be as forthright and dynamic as other mining houses. There is no doubt that the more honest and open management is, the better they will be rated in the market."

Recent talk that Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd and Gencor Ltd were salivating to snap up Gold Fields' mines hinted that the market had lost faith in current management to bring about necessary change, analysts said.

"On any given day not many (Gold Fields) shares trade. People are holding the shares they have on the basis that something has to happen. Everyone is waiting for the company to fall over and the question is when. The results may cause people to re-look quite aggressively," he said.
By 1218 GMT only 7,200 Gold Fields shares had changed hands, knocking 50 cents off the price to 130 rand per share.
Giese said that the group may have brought out all its "bad news" in the September quarter to smooth results in the December quarter -- a dividend paying quarter.
